name: Data Bars
basis: a bar chart per row, heights from brightness (how)

lumenary.blurb: The picture redrawn as rows of bar charts: every bar stands on its baseline, as tall as the picture is bright at that spot, in flat colour, in gold, or as blocks with a top and a side.

facts.bestOn: Bold shapes with strong light and shade

why: A bar chart turns a number into a height. A picture is a grid of numbers, one brightness for every spot, so it can be charted: slice it into rows, and in each row let a bar stand as tall as the picture is bright. From across the room the bars blend into the picture. Up close each row is a true chart of one strip of it.
how: Average the picture down to a grid, one cell for each bar.
Take each cell’s brightness, or its darkness, as the value.
Give every row its own baseline and raise a bar from it in proportion to the value.
Fill the bar with the cell’s colour, with a gold ramp, or as a block with a top and a side.
Rule the baselines and write the scale once.
history: William Playfair published the first bar chart in 1786, comparing Scotland’s trade with its partners, and in a few pages invented the line chart and later the pie chart as well. Bars became the plainest way to compare amounts. In the 2010s designers began treating data as material: charts built as physical objects, and “bar chart races” in which the bars overtake each other in time.
uses: Posters for data and finance events
terms: The line a bar stands on, where its value is zero.
A simple way to draw depth: the back is shifted sideways and up, with no vanishing point.
A picture made from marks whose size carries the tone.
paragraphs: The picture is averaged down to a grid with one cell for each bar. A cell’s value is its brightness, or one minus its brightness when bars are to stand tall on the dark parts. Each row of the grid has its own baseline, and a bar rises from it to a height in proportion to the value, never quite to nothing: the smallest bar is 3% of the full height. Read from a distance the rows of bars are a coarse halftone; read up close each row is an honest chart of the brightness along one strip of the picture.

The three looks differ only in how a bar is filled. Flat bars take the cell’s own colour, a little more saturated. Gold bars ignore the colour and read a ramp of five golds by the value, with a light stripe and a dark flank to suggest polished metal. Blocks add a side and a top, each a parallelogram pushed back and up by the same offset, one darker and one lighter than the face. That is an oblique projection, the kind used in spreadsheet charts.

equations.note: Bar height from the cell value v. H_full is 86% of the row height.
Gold look: the value picks a place on a ramp from dark bronze to pale gold.
Blocks: a point z behind the face is drawn to the right and half as far up.

presets.text: Gold bars on black suit an awards slide.
Blocks on paper look like a printed 3D chart.
Let the bars stand tall on the dark parts for a negative.
